title: Cat Behavior and Senses (2024 National Exam A)
content: Animals can express their needs using a lot of ways. For instance, almost all animals have distinct vocals that they rely on to either ask for help, scare away any dangerous animals or look for shelter. But cats are special creatures who possess amazing vocalization skills. They are able to have entire conversations with humans using mews and you're able to interpret it. If a pet cat is hungry, it will keep mewing to attract attention and find food. However, when a cat is looking for affection, they tend to produce stretched and soft mews. Mewing starts as soon as a baby cat is brought to life and uses it to get the mother's attention and be fed. Cats have many heightened senses, but their sense of smell is quite impressive. They use their noses to assess their environment and look out for any signs of danger. Your cat will likely smell your face and store the smell in its memory and use it to recognize you in the future. Dogs are known for their impressive fetching habit, but cats take this behavior up a notch. Many cats will find random objects outside and bring them to their owners. These adorable little hunters are just doing something that it's been in their nature since the beginning of time.

title: Digital Reading and Deep Thinking (2024 National Exam A)
content: Digital texts, audio and video all have educational roles, but reading and engaging with books remains the best way for individuals to improve their literacy skills and develop deep thinking abilities. Reading encourages engagement with language in ways that improve memory, comprehension and critical thinking. When students read physical books, they develop a spatial understanding of the text. They remember where information was located on the page, which helps them recall the content. This spatial memory is harder to develop with digital texts where the page layout constantly changes. Furthermore, reading books without hyperlinks or notifications allows for deeper focus and concentration. The reader can become fully absorbed in the narrative or argument. This sustained attention builds the capacity for complex thought that is essential for academic and professional success. Despite the convenience of digital devices, research consistently shows that students who read physical books score higher on reading comprehension tests and report greater enjoyment of reading. The tactile experience of holding a book, turning pages, and marking passages creates a physical connection to the text that enhances learning.

title: Urban Wildlife Adaptation (2024 National Exam A)
content: As cities expand and natural habitats shrink, wildlife species face increasing pressure to adapt or perish. Remarkably, some animals are not merely surviving in urban environments but are actually thriving. Scientists have discovered that urban foxes, raccoons, and birds are evolving new behaviors at unprecedented rates. City-dwelling birds, for instance, have begun singing at higher frequencies to be heard over traffic noise. Some species have even changed their breeding patterns to align with the artificial light and warmth of human settlements. Researchers at the University of Washington found that crows can remember human faces for years and will teach their offspring which humans are threats. This cultural transmission of knowledge is a sophisticated adaptation that helps urban wildlife navigate complex human-dominated landscapes. However, not all species can adapt so quickly. Specialist species that rely on specific food sources or habitats are particularly vulnerable to urbanization. The challenge for conservationists is to create urban green spaces that support biodiversity while accommodating the needs of growing human populations.

title: The Art of Being Alone (2023 National Exam A)
content: In a world that increasingly values connectivity and constant communication, the ability to be alone has become a rare and valuable skill. Solitude is not the same as loneliness. While loneliness is a negative state marked by a sense of isolation, solitude is a positive and constructive state of engagement with oneself. Many great thinkers and artists throughout history have emphasized the importance of solitude for creativity and self-discovery. The philosopher Descartes famously did his best thinking in bed, away from the distractions of Paris. The poet Wordsworth wandered the Lake District alone, finding inspiration in nature's quiet beauty. Psychologists today confirm that spending time alone can improve concentration, boost creativity, and help individuals develop a stronger sense of identity. However, solitude must be balanced with social connection. Humans are inherently social beings, and prolonged isolation can indeed lead to loneliness and mental health problems. The key is to cultivate the ability to be comfortable alone while also maintaining meaningful relationships. This balance allows individuals to bring their best selves to their interactions with others.

title: The Science of Nostalgia (2023 National Exam A)
content: Nostalgia was once considered a mental disorder, a form of homesickness so severe that it could be fatal. Eighteenth-century physicians viewed it as a disease of the mind, prescribing everything from leeches to trips to the Swiss Alps as cures. Today, however, scientists have discovered that nostalgia is not only harmless but actually beneficial for mental health. Research conducted by psychologists at the University of Southampton has shown that nostalgic memories can increase feelings of social connectedness, boost self-esteem, and even provide a sense of meaning in life. When people think about positive memories from their past, their brains release dopamine, the same neurotransmitter associated with pleasure and reward. This explains why listening to a song from one's teenage years or revisiting a childhood home can produce such intense feelings of warmth and comfort. Nostalgia also serves an important psychological function during times of transition or uncertainty. When facing challenges, people naturally turn to memories of times when they felt safe and supported. This mental retreat provides emotional resilience and helps individuals cope with present difficulties. However, excessive nostalgia can become problematic if it leads people to idealize the past at the expense of engaging with the present. The healthiest approach is to use nostalgic memories as a source of strength while remaining open to creating new positive experiences.

title: Gardener's Year-Round Guide (2022 National Exam A)
content: Successful gardening requires understanding the seasonal rhythms of plants. In spring, focus on soil preparation and planting. Test your soil's pH level and add compost to improve fertility. This is the ideal time to plant cool-season vegetables like lettuce, peas, and spinach. As temperatures rise in early summer, switch to warm-season crops such as tomatoes, peppers, and cucumbers. Consistent watering becomes crucial during hot periods; early morning irrigation minimizes evaporation and helps prevent fungal diseases. Autumn is harvest time for most vegetables, but it's also the season for planting spring-flowering bulbs and preparing perennials for winter. Mulching garden beds with straw or leaves protects root systems from freezing temperatures. Winter gardening is often overlooked but can be productive. Cold frames and greenhouses extend the growing season, allowing for fresh greens even in January. Use this quiet season to plan next year's garden, order seeds, and maintain tools. Keeping a garden journal throughout the year helps track what varieties performed well and which pests were problematic, enabling continuous improvement.

title: The History of Tea (2021 Sichuan Exam)
content: Tea has been cultivated in China for over 4,000 years, making it one of the oldest beverages in continuous use. According to legend, Emperor Shen Nong discovered tea in 2737 BC when leaves from a wild tree blew into his pot of boiling water. The resulting brew was refreshing and invigorating, and tea cultivation began shortly thereafter. During the Tang Dynasty, tea drinking became an art form, with elaborate ceremonies and specialized utensils. The scholar Lu Yu wrote the Classic of Tea, the first comprehensive treatise on tea cultivation and preparation. Tea spread to Japan in the ninth century, where it evolved into the ritualized tea ceremony that continues today. European traders first encountered tea in the sixteenth century, and by the eighteenth century, it had become Britain's national drink. The British East India Company established vast tea plantations in India and Ceylon to meet growing European demand. Today, tea is the second most consumed beverage in the world after water, with global production exceeding 6 million metric tons annually. Different varieties black, green, oolong, and white result from varying degrees of oxidation and processing.

title: Language and Thought (2020 Sichuan Exam)
content: The relationship between language and thought has fascinated philosophers and scientists for centuries. Does language shape the way we think, or does thought exist independently of language? The Sapir-Whorf hypothesis, proposed in the early twentieth century, suggests that the structure of a language affects its speakers' world view. For example, some languages have multiple words for what English speakers would simply call 'snow,' and speakers of these languages reportedly perceive snow differently. However, modern research has challenged strong versions of this hypothesis. Studies show that while language may influence thought in subtle ways, fundamental cognitive abilities such as spatial reasoning and numerical understanding exist independently of language. Recent neurological research using brain imaging has revealed that language and thought activate different but interconnected brain regions. This suggests a more nuanced relationship in which language serves as a tool for expressing and refining thoughts rather than determining them entirely. The debate continues, but most researchers now agree that language and thought influence each other in complex, bidirectional ways.

title: Travel Destination Guide (2019 Sichuan Exam)
content: Nestled in the heart of the Canadian Rockies, Banff National Park offers visitors an unparalleled wilderness experience. Established in 1885, it is Canada's oldest national park and a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The park encompasses 6,641 square kilometers of mountainous terrain, featuring turquoise glacial lakes, dense pine forests, and snow-capped peaks. Lake Louise, with its emerald waters reflecting the surrounding Victoria Glacier, is the park's most photographed location. Moraine Lake, equally stunning but less crowded, offers excellent hiking trails ranging from easy lakeside walks to challenging mountain ascents. Wildlife is abundant; visitors frequently spot elk, deer, black bears, and bighorn sheep. The town of Banff provides accommodation options from luxury resorts to budget hostels, along with restaurants serving locally sourced cuisine. The best time to visit depends on your interests: summer offers hiking, canoeing, and wildlife viewing, while winter transforms the park into a skiing and ice-climbing paradise. Park entrance fees are $10 per adult per day. An annual pass, valid for all Canadian national parks, costs $72.

title: The Power of Failure (2019 Sichuan Exam)
content: Failure is an essential part of learning and growth, yet modern society often stigmatizes it. From an early age, children are taught to avoid mistakes, and educational systems reward correct answers while penalizing errors. This approach, while well-intentioned, may actually hinder intellectual development. Recent research in educational psychology suggests that productive failure deliberately allowing students to struggle with complex problems before receiving instruction leads to deeper understanding and better long-term retention. When students wrestle with difficult concepts, they generate multiple hypotheses and explore different solution paths, even if they don't initially arrive at the correct answer. This process builds cognitive flexibility and problem-solving skills. History is filled with examples of failure preceding success. Thomas Edison famously conducted thousands of unsuccessful experiments before inventing the practical light bulb. J.K. Rowling's Harry Potter manuscript was rejected by twelve publishers before finding a home. These stories illustrate that failure is not the opposite of success but rather a stepping stone toward it. The key is to reframe failure as feedback, extracting lessons from setbacks and applying them to future endeavors.

title: The Science of Sleep (2018 Sichuan Exam)
content: Sleep is not merely a period of rest but a complex biological process essential for physical and mental health. During sleep, the brain performs critical maintenance tasks, consolidating memories, clearing toxins, and reorganizing neural connections. Research has identified two main types of sleep: rapid eye movement (REM) sleep and non-REM sleep, each serving distinct functions. Non-REM sleep, which occupies about 75% of total sleep time, is associated with physical restoration. During deep non-REM sleep, blood pressure drops, breathing slows, and blood flow to muscles increases, facilitating tissue repair and growth. REM sleep, characterized by vivid dreaming and brain activity similar to wakefulness, is crucial for cognitive functions including creativity and emotional regulation. Chronic sleep deprivation has been linked to numerous health problems, including obesity, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and depression. Despite these well-documented risks, surveys indicate that nearly one-third of adults regularly get less than the recommended seven to nine hours of sleep per night. Modern lifestyle factors excessive screen time, irregular work schedules, and high stress levels contribute to this sleep crisis. Experts recommend establishing consistent sleep schedules, creating dark and cool sleeping environments, and limiting caffeine and alcohol consumption to improve sleep quality.

title: Biodiversity Conservation (2017 Sichuan Exam)
content: Biodiversity the variety of life on Earth at all levels, from genes to ecosystems is declining at an alarming rate. Scientists estimate that species are going extinct at 100 to 1,000 times the natural background rate, primarily due to human activities. Habitat destruction, pollution, climate change, and invasive species are the major drivers of this biodiversity crisis. The consequences extend far beyond the loss of individual species. Ecosystems with high biodiversity are more resilient to environmental changes and provide essential services such as pollination, water purification, and carbon storage. The economic value of these ecosystem services has been estimated at $125 trillion annually. Conservation efforts have traditionally focused on establishing protected areas, and while these remain important, they are insufficient alone. Emerging approaches include habitat corridors that connect fragmented populations, community-based conservation that engages local people as stewards, and market-based incentives that reward sustainable land use. Genetic technologies such as seed banking and assisted reproduction offer additional tools for preserving endangered species. Ultimately, addressing the biodiversity crisis requires transformative changes in how societies produce and consume resources.

title: The Value of Reading Classics (2016 Sichuan Exam)
content: In an age of instant information and social media, the sustained attention required for reading classical literature may seem antiquated. Yet classic works endure for reasons that transcend their historical periods. These texts address universal themes love, mortality, ambition, morality that remain relevant across centuries and cultures. Reading classics develops critical thinking skills in ways that scanning online articles cannot. The complex narratives and ambiguous characters of great literature demand active interpretation, forcing readers to weigh evidence, consider multiple perspectives, and make reasoned judgments. Furthermore, classical texts provide cultural literacy, the shared references and allusions that enable sophisticated communication. A person unfamiliar with Shakespeare cannot fully appreciate how his phrases have permeated everyday English. Similarly, understanding references to Greek mythology enriches comprehension of Western art, politics, and psychology. Some educators argue that the canon of classics should be expanded to include works from diverse traditions, and this is a valid critique. However, the underlying value of engaging with demanding, complex texts remains unchanged. The discipline of close reading, the expansion of vocabulary, and the development of empathy through encountering different worldviews these benefits make classics worth the effort.
